title: Goals & Money Habits
description: Turn wishes into numbers, and numbers into habits.
wolfLine: A goal without a number is just a wish.

smart-goal.definition: A goal that’s Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound: exactly what, how much, and by when.
smart-goal.example: Save $1,500 for an emergency fund in 10 months.

time-horizon.definition: How far away a goal is. Short-term is under a year, mid-term is 1 to 5 years, long-term is more than 5.
time-horizon.example: A car in 3 years has a mid-term time horizon.

present-bias.definition: The pull to choose a smaller reward now over a bigger one later.
present-bias.example: Spending your trip savings on a sale today.

lessons.title: Goals That Work
lessons.summary: Turn “save more” into a number and a date.

steps.context: A [[SMART goal|smart-goal]] is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. In plain words: exactly what, how much, and by when.
steps.prompt: Which is a SMART goal?
choices: Save $3,000 for a car down payment by next December
steps.explain: What, how much, by when. The other two can’t be measured.

steps.prompt: SMART or vague?
items: Save $500 for a laptop by March
Build a $1,500 emergency fund in 10 months
Put $50 into savings every payday this year

steps.prompt: Goal: $1,500 in 10 months. How much a month?
Writing a goal down and checking it every month makes you more likely to hit it.
steps.explain: What gets checked gets done.

steps.prompt: Your $1,500 goal is at $600 after 6 months. Are you on track?
steps.explain: $150 × 6 = $900 planned. You’re $300 behind.

steps.prompt: To still finish on time in the last 4 months, how much a month do you need now?

lessons.title: Short, Mid and Long Term
lessons.summary: When you need the money changes where it should live.

steps.context: A goal’s [[time horizon]] is how far away it is. Short-term: under a year. Mid-term: 1 to 5 years. Long-term: more than 5 years.
steps.prompt: Saving for a car in 3 years is…
steps.explain: Between 1 and 5 years away.

steps.prompt: Sort the goals by time horizon.
Where should money for a short-term goal live?
choices: Somewhere safe and easy to reach, like savings
steps.explain: If you need it soon, it can’t be at risk.

steps.prompt: Long-term goals can wait until you’re older.
steps.explain: Long goals need the most time. Starting early is the cheat code.

steps.prompt: A $3,600 goal in 3 years. How much a month?
Money is tight. Which goal do you fund first?
steps.explain: Protection first, fun second.

lessons.title: What Comes First
lessons.summary: Every goal wants your money. Put them in line.

steps.title: A common order
steps.body: Every goal wants your money. A common order: keep the lights on, build a small cushion, grow it to a real safety net, then work on bigger goals. You can work on several at once, but the order tells you what wins when money is short.

steps.prompt: Put these in the usual priority order.
items: Grow it to 3 months of essential expenses
Save for bigger goals like a car or a trip
steps.explain: Survive, cushion, safety net, then goals.

steps.prompt: You have $1,000 spare and no emergency fund yet. Best move?
steps.explain: The cushion protects every other goal.

steps.prompt: You can work on more than one goal at a time by splitting each paycheck.
steps.explain: Splitting keeps every goal moving.

steps.prompt: You save $300 a month: 60% to the emergency fund, 40% to a trip. How much goes to the trip?
A goal stops mattering to you. What now?
choices: Move its money to a goal that does matter
steps.explain: Goals change. Let the money follow.

lessons.title: Small Habits, Big Numbers
lessons.summary: Tiny daily amounts, huge yearly totals.

steps.context: Tiny daily amounts become big yearly ones. Multiply by 365.
steps.prompt: $4 a day for a year. What’s the total?
$10 a week for 10 years, which is 520 weeks?

steps.context: Habits stick when they’re easy and automatic. Make the good choice the default.
steps.prompt: Which habit is easiest to keep?
choices: Remembering to save whatever is left
Saving only when you feel rich
steps.explain: Automatic means it happens even on bad weeks.

steps.prompt: Rounding every card purchase up to the next dollar and saving the change can add up.
steps.explain: Many banks will do it for you.

steps.prompt: Round-ups average $0.45 a purchase, and you make 60 purchases a month. How much do you save a month?
You missed your savings transfer one month. Best response?
steps.explain: One miss is a blip. Quitting is the real cost.

steps.context: [[Present bias]] is the pull to choose a reward now over a bigger one later.
steps.prompt: Which is present bias?
choices: Spending your trip savings on a sale today
steps.explain: Today’s deal beat next month’s trip.

steps.prompt: Why is “it’s only $5” dangerous?
steps.explain: Twenty “only $5” moments is $100.

steps.prompt: Treating a tax refund as free money and spending it all is a common trap.
steps.explain: A refund is your own money coming back. Give it a job like any other.

steps.prompt: Your friends eat out a lot and you feel the pressure. Healthy move?
choices: Suggest cheaper plans sometimes, or join less often
Go every time and stop saving
steps.explain: Friends who matter will take a picnic.

steps.prompt: Trap or smart move?
items: Buying it because everyone has one
Waiting a day before a big buy
Spending a bonus in a week

steps.prompt: What’s the best defense against brain traps?
choices: Rules decided in advance, like a budget and a waiting rule
steps.explain: Decide when you’re calm, not when you’re in the store.

lessons.title: Your Weekly Money Date
lessons.summary: Ten minutes a week keeps the whole plan on track.

steps.title: Ten minutes, once a week
steps.body: Once a week, take ten minutes: check your balance and pending transactions, look at spending by category, move money if a category ran hot, and nudge your goals.

steps.prompt: Put the weekly check-in in order.
items: Check your balance and pending transactions
Move money between categories if needed
steps.explain: Where you stand, what happened, fix it, look ahead.

steps.prompt: A weekly check-in only matters when something went wrong.
steps.explain: It’s how you catch things before they go wrong.

steps.prompt: When’s the best time for a money date?
choices: The same time every week, like Sunday evening
Only when you feel like it
steps.explain: A fixed time turns it into a habit.

steps.prompt: At your check-in you see $45 on snacks this week. The budget was $25. What do you do?
choices: Move $20 from fun to food and plan better next week
steps.explain: Patch it, then plan.

steps.prompt: Ten minutes a week for 52 weeks. About how many hours a year is that? Round to the nearest hour.
steps.explain: 10 × 52 = 520 minutes. 520 ÷ 60 = 8.7, about 9 hours a year.

lessons.title: Morgan’s Plan
lessons.summary: Three goals, one paycheck. Make it fit.

story.title: One year, three goals
story.body:
Morgan takes home **$3,000** a month. Needs (rent, food, transport, phone) cost **$1,850**. Morgan wants three things this year:

A **$1,200** starter emergency fund within 12 months. A **$900** trip in August, eight months away. A new laptop for **$720**, a year from now.

Right now Morgan spends whatever isn’t needed, about **$1,150** a month on wants, and saves nothing.

steps.prompt: How much a month for the trip, eight months away?
How much a month for the laptop, 12 months away?
And for the $1,200 emergency fund in 12 months?
What’s Morgan’s total monthly saving for all three goals?
After needs and goals, how much is left for wants?
Plan Morgan’s month. Needs are fixed, and goals need at least $300 (rounded up from $272.50 to leave some slack).
steps.explain: Every plan works if needs are covered, goals get at least $300, and nothing is left without a job.

lessons.title: Your First Money Plan
lessons.summary: Everything from this section, on one page.

steps.title: Everything in one plan
steps.body: You’ve learned to track, budget, bank, save and spend smart. A money plan puts it on one page: what comes in, what goes out, what you’re building, and the habits that keep it running.

steps.prompt: Put your money plan in order.
items: Pay yourself first: savings and goals
steps.explain: In, out, future you, fun, follow-up.

steps.prompt: Which account setup supports the plan?
choices: Checking for bills, a separate savings account, alerts on
One account for everything, no alerts
steps.explain: Separate pots and early warnings.

steps.context: Put it all together: give every dollar of one month a job.
steps.prompt: Plan a $2,800 take-home month. Rent and phone are fixed. Groceries need at least $300, transport at least $150, savings at least $300.
steps.explain: Needs covered, savings protected, every dollar given a job.

steps.prompt: A money plan should change when your life changes.
steps.explain: New job, new city, new goal: new plan.

steps.prompt: Which one habit holds the whole plan together?
steps.explain: A plan you look at is a plan that works.

lessons.title: Sharpen Up
lessons.summary: Smart repetition on what you’re closest to forgetting.

lessons.title: Den Trial: Goals & Habits
lessons.summary: 8 questions. Three strikes and you’re out.

steps.prompt: A $2,400 goal in 12 months. How much a month?
A home deposit in 4 years has what time horizon?
steps.explain: Between 1 and 5 years.

steps.prompt: Choosing a sale today over your planned trip is an example of present bias.
steps.explain: Now beat later.

steps.prompt: Put these in priority order.
steps.explain: Survive, cushion, then build.
